name: Tara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at two, so I'm in the changing room behind the dish pit by quarter to. First job is my prep for the second grill at Marrow, which is a big steak and grill place on the river: portion the steaks, make the garlic butter, slice about eight kilos of onions. Service runs six till eleven, and on a Saturday we'll do two hundred covers, which means two hundred people fed. I'm still learning, so our head chef, Dario, checks nearly everything I send.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rush, when the ticket rail is full and nobody has time to talk and somehow it all goes out. I left school at sixteen, and this is the first job where I feel I'm getting better at something with my hands. What wears me out is the heat and the standing, and the burns up my forearms. And the split shifts on Sundays, which the union is fighting about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what I'd expect. The AI talk hasn't touched our kitchen anyway, apart from the booking screen at the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the union group chat. Half the people in there were sure robots were coming for the line. I'd say fine, now let's get back to what actually hurts us, like split shifts and where the service charge goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get the time I need, because I'm not quick yet. Dario still sends back maybe one steak in ten from me. If AI turns out to be hype, I keep burning my forearms on the second grill and learning the job slowly, which suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Keep my shifts, keep paying my union dues, and keep the rent from my nan's flat going into savings. Maybe by next summer I'd ask Dario for a proper go on the first grill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit let down too, because people kept promising AI would fix the rota mess, and in this picture it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rota. Would even a small bit of AI change anything in your kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our manager, already makes the rota on some app, and it's no better than when she did it on paper. Maybe her ordering gets a bit faster. Nothing on my side of the pass changes, because software can't turn a steak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And money-wise, how does the next year look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. My nan left me a small flat, and the rent from it is about thirteen hundred a month, which nearly all goes into the bank. I've got more than a year of costs saved, and Noor, my partner, drives buses, which is steady work.

say: I'd tell the **union chat** that the robot panic was overblown.
I'd push to get talk back to **split shifts** and the service charge.
think: I need **time** to get good, because I'm still slow on the grill.
With my nan's **flat** and savings, a quiet world is a safe one for me.
do: Keep my **shifts** and union dues exactly as they are.
Put the **rent** from the flat into savings every month.
Ask Dario for a turn on the **first grill** by next summer.
feel: Mostly **relieved** that nothing changes on the line.
A little **let down** that the rota mess stays unfixed.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I keep burning my forearms on the second grill and learning the job slowly, which suits me fine.
fieldNote: Her **inherited flat** gives her a safety net most junior cooks don't have.
She frames work problems as **union fights**, not technology ones.
She openly says she is **slow**, which makes extra time feel like a gift to her.

steps.text: Keep working the second grill and ask for first grill by summer
Bank the rent from her nan's flat every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly, it says. That's the bit I'd be watching, because the thinking stuff isn't really my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses will use this to squeeze us, same as always. I'd post that any new machine on the line should be agreed with the union first. And I'd say booking and ordering going to software means fewer jobs for the front-of-house girls, not for us yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm alright for a few years, but I'm not proud of why. Dario does the thinking parts, the menu and the ordering, and I just cook. If AI takes the booking and the ordering, the cooks who only cook are safe for now, and I'm one of the ones who only cooks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union branch meeting this year, not just the odd one. I'd keep stacking the flat money, maybe push my savings up to eighteen months. I won't touch the AI apps myself, I just don't trust them, and I don't need them to sear a steak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me this year, but I'd be watching every delivery van at the back door in case it's carrying a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi on the fryer, because chain places already have frying robots that drop the baskets. And Leanne, who takes bookings and answers the phone, because that's exactly the stuff on your card. I'd want the union to fight for both of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you won't use AI tools at all. What if Dario asked you to use one for prep lists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it if he made me, but I'd hate it. I write my prep list in a little notebook in my apron, and I'd keep the notebook as well. I'm slow with screens and I don't want to be slow at two things.

say: I'd warn that bosses will use AI to **squeeze staff**.
I'd say every new **machine** on the line needs union agreement first.
think: I'm **safe for now** because I only cook, not order or plan.
The **fryer** and the front desk will feel it before me.
do: Go to every **union branch meeting** this year.
Grow my **savings** from about twelve to eighteen months.
Keep my **paper notebook** for prep lists instead of apps.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching the back door for new machines.
S1.quote: If AI takes the booking and the ordering, the cooks who only cook are safe for now, and I'm one of the ones who only cooks.
fieldNote: She sees her **low thinking-AI exposure** clearly and feels slightly guilty about it.
Her first concern is **colleagues** on the fryer and front desk.
She would comply with AI under orders but keep her **notebook** as a quiet protest.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting and raise the fryer robots
Build savings from twelve to eighteen months of costs
Keep writing prep lists in her apron notebook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's 2028, and then robots by 2031. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, not promises. I'd be on the march, I'd be telling everyone to join a union now, while we still have something to bargain with. Nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the AI part barely touches me, but the robot part finishes me. In 2028 Priya's ordering and rota go to a computer, fine. When the robots arrive in 2031 and one robot can work a grill all night without burns, a slow junior cook like me is first out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get on the union's tech committee, because there has to be a deal on how robots come in, like retraining money or notice. I'd stop spending on anything big and keep every penny of the flat rent. And I'd think about whether Noor and I should keep the flat as our own home instead of renting it out, because owning where you live matters if work disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I've only just found something I'm getting good at, and it's got a three-year clock on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're lucky, because of the flat, and that I hate that luck is what's saving us. Noor would say buses go driverless too. Then we'd both go quiet, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're slow to learn new things. What would those three years be for, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting as good as I can at the grill, so I'm the last one they let go. And fighting, honestly. I'm not going to learn to programme robots, that's not me, but I can stand in a picket line.

say: I'd demand **laws**, not promises, and march for them.
I'd tell every cook to **join a union** while they can bargain.
think: The 2028 AI barely touches me, but the **2031 robots** end my job.
As a **slow junior**, I'd be first to go.
do: Join the union's **tech committee** to win notice and retraining money.
Stop **big spending** and keep all the flat's rent.
Talk with Noor about **living in the flat** instead of renting it.
feel: **Sick** that her new skill has a three-year clock on it.
**Grateful** for the flat, and angry that luck decides it.
S2.quote: When the robots arrive in 2031 and one robot can work a grill all night without burns, a slow junior cook like me is first out the door.
fieldNote: She separates the **two dates** precisely: AI barely matters, robots end her job.
Her plan is **collective**, not personal retraining.
The **flat** turns from income into a possible home in her thinking.

steps.text: Join the union's tech committee and push for robot notice rules
Cancel big purchases and save all the flat's rent
Discuss moving into her nan's flat with Noor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. That's different, there's time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that we need rules, but I'd say it calmer. Five years is long enough for a government to actually do something if people push. I'd be pushing for a law that a restaurant has to pay into a retraining fund for every cook a robot replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be thirty-five when the robots come, and properly good on the grill by then, which still might not save me. Five years gives a government time to act, so in 2034 there's nobody left to blame except the people who did nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, nothing very different, just more union work and saving. Around 2031, when the AI part lands, I'd watch what happens to Priya and the office people. If they get wiped out, that's my warning, and I'd start looking at jobs robots can't easily do, maybe care work like my aunt does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slower kind. Like knowing a big bill is due but not until next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Is that something you'd really consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My aunt works in a care home and she says they're always short. It's people, not plates, and I'm not sure a robot is allowed to wash somebody's grandad. But I'd hate leaving the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first in your spending, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays. Noor and I go somewhere hot every spring, and that would stop the year AI arrives. I'd keep the flat whatever happens.

say: I'd call for a **retraining fund** paid by restaurants using robots.
I'd say five years is enough time for **government** to act.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** and good at the grill, but still replaceable.
If politicians waste the warning, it's on **them**.
do: Keep up **union work** and saving through the next five years.
Watch the **office staff** in 2031 as an early warning.
Look into **care work** like my aunt's if the warning comes true.
feel: **Anxious**, like a big bill that isn't due yet.
S3.quote: Five years gives a government time to act, so in 2034 there's nobody left to blame except the people who did nothing.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her anger into a **policy demand**.
She'd use the **2031 AI wave** as a signal before robots reach her.
**Care work** is her only escape idea, and she's reluctant.

steps.text: Lobby for a restaurant-funded retraining fund for replaced cooks
Ask her aunt about care home jobs in 2031
Stop the yearly spring holiday the year AI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be forty when the robots come. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Shorter weeks, retraining, a share of the savings going back to the workers. I'd say that in the union and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably relax too much. Ten years feels like forever to someone who's twenty-seven, and that's exactly the trap for a cook like me. I know myself, I'd say I'll sort it in five years and then not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and try to get to first grill and then maybe sous chef, which is second in charge. I'd keep the savings going and pay off whatever needs fixing in the flat. Around 2036 I'd look again, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. More like worrying about getting old than worrying about next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not act until it's late. What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in my own kitchen. If Marrow bought even one machine for the fryer, I'd take it seriously. A news story won't do it, I don't read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what you and Noor plan for the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might think about kids by then, honestly, and I'd want them in a world where cooking is still a job. But that's not a decision I'd make because of robots.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for doing it badly.
I'd back **shorter weeks** and a share of the savings for workers.
think: I'd **relax too much** and leave planning far too late.
Only a machine in **my own kitchen** would make me move.
do: Work towards **first grill** and then sous chef.
Keep **saving** and fix up the flat.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like worrying about getting old.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever to someone who's twenty-seven, and that's exactly the trap for a cook like me.
fieldNote: She is **honest** that a long warning would make her lazy.
Her trigger is **seeing a machine**, not reading news.
Her **politics** stay steady across every timeline.

steps.text: Work towards first grill and then sous chef at Marrow
Vote for a party promising shorter weeks and retraining
Keep saving the flat's rent every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. The thinking part I don't care about, but robots on the line three years later, while I'm still slow, that's the one. My nan's flat is the only reason I'm not scared, and I hate that luck decides who's safe. What would help is the union getting a deal in writing before the first machine arrives: notice, pay to retrain, and a say in which jobs go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. If it's the restaurant, the cooks lose. If cooks had a share, it'd be a different story, and nobody ever asks that.

headlineQuote: My nan's flat is the only reason I'm not scared, and I hate that luck decides who's safe.
portrait: Tara is a **junior grill cook** at Marrow, a busy steak restaurant, still slow and still learning.
An inherited **flat** and over a year of savings make her money secure.
She sees every change as a **union fight** and avoids AI tools herself.
She feels **calm** if AI stalls, but the **2031 robots** would leave her anxious.
With **ten years**, she admits she'd probably leave planning too late.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach her grill while she's still **slow**.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** in writing before robots arrive: notice, **retraining pay** and a say.
